Dear Councilmember Garcia and Policy Aide — prepared on behalf of the Local Retailers Coalition, I write to share retailer concerns about the proposed 10¢ single‑use plastic bag fee: we support the city’s environmental goals but urge adjustments to avoid disproportionate burdens on local businesses.  

The city staff memo and municipal evaluations cited therein (e.g., San Jose and Seattle case studies summarized by staff) indicate likely operational and financial impacts for small and medium retailers — longer checkout times, point‑of‑sale software updates and labeling costs, added staff training and customer interactions, and compliance/admin burdens that are proportionally larger for independent grocers and convenience stores.  

Different customer groups will feel the effects unequally: lower‑income shoppers and customers with mobility, language, or work‑hour constraints are more likely to be sensitive to added costs or to lack reusable bags (this is reported in customer‑response sections of the staff memo), while the research staff summarized also shows the fee can reduce bag use and litter in many municipal evaluations.  

To reduce retail burdens we respectfully request Council consider concrete options supported by municipal precedent and staff analysis: targeted exemptions for very small retailers or specified transaction types, permitting retailers to retain a modest portion of collected fees to cover administration, a 6–12 month phased implementation with clear IT/compliance guidance, and directing net revenue to city‑run free reusable bag distribution and public outreach.

rounds.response:
Prepared on behalf of the Local Retailers Coalition for Councilmember Garcia and Policy Aide: concise briefing on tradeoffs in the proposed 10¢ single‑use plastic bag fee.  

Summary of likely impacts (based on the city staff memo, the Riverton addendum, the regional comparison, and municipal evaluations cited therein): retailers—particularly independent grocers and small convenience stores—are likely to see operational and financial impacts such as longer checkout times, more staff–customer interactions and disputes, point‑of‑sale/IT and labeling updates, staff training, and added compliance/admin costs; customers—lower‑income shoppers, people with mobility or time constraints, and limited‑English customers are more likely to be disproportionately affected; city revenues/administration—fees can produce modest net revenue but require city oversight, merchant reporting, and enforcement resources; environmental outcomes—the cited evidence shows fees commonly reduce single‑use bag use and local litter in the short–to–medium term (stronger consensus), while longer‑term behavior change and substitution effects are more mixed.  

Design levers and effects on retailer burden (evidence strength noted): coverage/exemptions—targeted exemptions or size‑based thresholds reduce compliance burdens for the smallest retailers (supported by municipal precedents); retailer retention of a modest per‑bag administrative share lowers net costs to merchants (used in some cities); revenue use—dedicating net revenue to city‑run free reusable bag distribution and retailer outreach/training mitigates customer impacts and eases transitions; implementation timetable—phased rollouts (6–12 months) with clear IT/pos guidance and city support materially reduce startup costs (Riverton experience and staff memo); reporting/compliance—simple, standardized reporting and minimal paperwork reduce ongoing burdens, though enforcement approaches and costs vary across cities (evidence more mixed).  

Recommended package to present at the work session that preserves environmental benefits while reducing retailer burden: 1) adopt targeted exemptions or a size threshold for the smallest independent retailers; 2) allow retailers to retain a modest administrative portion of the fee; 3) require a 6–12 month phased implementation with city technical assistance and clear POS specifications; and 4) dedicate net revenues to free reusable bag distribution and retailer outreach/training — these steps are grounded in the staff memo, Riverton addendum, and cited municipal case studies and would keep burdens proportionate while maintaining most of the fee’s litter‑reduction benefits.
